questions.stem: The board's reassurances were {1}: the market had absorbed the merger news weeks earlier, and any further statement risked unsettling shareholders so {2} that a routine footnote in the quarterly filing could touch off a selloff.
questions.explanation: Because the news had already been absorbed, one more statement is simply more than the situation required — superfluous; indispensable and imperative both assert the opposite. The second blank must explain why speech is dangerous, and skittish supplies the hair trigger, a reaction wildly out of proportion to its cause; imperturbable shareholders would ignore a footnote entirely.

questions.stem: Reviewers admired the biography's {1} handling of the campaign years — no ledger unopened, no surviving correspondent left uninterviewed — yet regretted that it never paused for a {2} chapter setting those years against the politics of the century as a whole.
questions.explanation: The dashes itemize full coverage of the process — everywhere gone, everything checked — which is precisely thorough, while cursory and haphazard describe the opposite habit. The second blank names what such coverage still lacks, a wide vantage on the whole; meticulous and punctilious would only repeat the fine-grained care the book already has, whereas synoptic is about breadth of view rather than fineness of finish.

questions.stem: Having already made the same argument at length in his opening remarks, the senator found the rebuttal he had prepared for the afternoon session {1}, and he sat down without delivering a word of it.
questions.explanation: Since the ground has been covered already, the speech is one item more than the occasion required, and both superfluous and redundant yield that sense of a thing not needed because it adds nothing new. Indispensable and imperative form a tempting pair but assert exactly the reverse; premature is contradicted by "already," and injudicious would fault the speech's wisdom rather than its necessity.

questions.stem: Once observers across the continent began wiring their barometer readings to a single office, a forecaster could at last draw one {1} chart on which the whole pressure field stood visible as it had been at a single hour.
questions.explanation: The chart's virtue is width and simultaneity — every region seen together from above — which is what synoptic denotes, and meteorologists use the term in exactly this sense. Exhaustive is the nearest trap, but it claims completeness of detail rather than a whole surveyed at once, and distilled would suggest the opposite operation, boiling the data down rather than laying it all out.

questions.stem: Placid enough under saddle to be trusted with a beginner, the mare was nonetheless {1}: a wheelbarrow tipping over three paddocks away would send her careening down the fence line.
questions.explanation: The sentence insists the animal is ordinarily calm and then supplies a trivial trigger and an explosive response, which is the signature of skittish: reactivity out of all proportion to the threat. Timorous, the closest competitor, names a settled fearful disposition and is ruled out by "placid enough to be trusted with a beginner"; craven implies moral cowardice, which no horse can be charged with.

questions.stem: The new director's first act was to commission a {1} survey of the museum's holdings — not another inventory of a single wing, but one account in which the entire collection could be seen together — a project her predecessor, {2} about anything that might expose past deaccessions, had quietly shelved twice.
questions.explanation: The appositive contrasts the survey not with an incomplete count but with a piecemeal one, so what is wanted is breadth and simultaneity of view: synoptic, where exhaustive would promise fullness of detail without the single vantage. The predecessor's repeated shelving is flinching rather than reasoning, which skittish captures; imperturbable and sanguine would both describe someone untroubled by the prospect and so explain nothing.

rejects.problem: Three positive options are mutually substitutable: thorough, meticulous, and exhaustive. The intended pair is presumably thorough/exhaustive (completeness), with meticulous as a distractor meaning "painstakingly careful about detail" — but the sentence does not enforce that distinction. "Every ledger re-audited" and "every lead run to ground" support painstaking care just as well as comprehensive scope, and thorough/meticulous are near-synonyms in ordinary usage. A test-taker choosing meticulous + exhaustive (or meticulous + thorough) produces a sentence of essentially the same meaning and would be marked wrong. Fix by removing meticulous, or by adding a cue that isolates scope over care (e.g., contrasting the original inquiry's narrow remit).
rejects.stem: The commission's final report was {1}: every witness re-interviewed, every ledger re-audited, every lead the original inquiry had abandoned run to ground.

rejects.problem: The logic (one clerk could have done the whole job, so a third auditor is one more body than the work requires) points to "superfluous" — exceeding what is needed — and "indispensable" (opposite) and "dilatory" (slow; unrelated) are clearly out. The defect is that "extraneous" is also defensible: in standard usage it means "not forming an essential or vital part" and is routinely treated as a synonym of "superfluous" (the two are a classic Sentence Equivalence pair). Nothing in the sentence forces the excess-in-number sense over the not-essential sense — the "however capable he proved" clause does no discriminating work, since capability is irrelevant to both readings. A reasonable test-taker could pick "extraneous" and be marked wrong. To fix, replace "extraneous" with a word that cannot mean "unnecessary" (e.g., "meticulous", "peripheral" is also risky — better "officious" or "ancillary"-free choice), or convert the item to Sentence Equivalence with superfluous/extraneous as the intended pair. ("Gratuitous" is a weaker distractor — it means unwarranted/uncalled-for and normally modifies acts or remarks, not a person.)
rejects.stem: One clerk could have reconciled the parish accounts in a morning, so the third auditor the vestry appointed, however capable he proved, was simply {1}.
